title: KV Cache
summary: Store keys and values from processed tokens so each new token costs O(1) instead of recomputation.
details: During generation, the transformer recomputes attention over all previous tokens unless their key/value projections are cached. The KV cache stores K and V per layer per token, turning each decode step into a cheap append-and-attend. Cache size grows linearly with sequence length and batch size — for a 70B model at 32K context it can exceed tens of GB — which is why PagedAttention, quantization, and prefix caching exist. Every serving engine implements it; it is the single most important inference optimization.
benefit: Turns O(n^2) per-token recompute into O(1) appends

demo.title: KV cache size math
demo.program:
layers, hidden, kv_ratio = 32, 4096, 0.25  # GQA
bytes_per_token = 2 * layers * hidden * kv_ratio * 2  # K+V, fp16
for seq, batch in [(4096, 1), (32768, 8)]:
    gb = bytes_per_token * seq * batch / 1e9
    print(f"seq={seq} batch={batch}: {gb:.1f} GB KV cache")

title: Continuous Batching
summary: Batch at the iteration level, not the request level — fill every freed slot the moment it opens.
details: Static batching waits for the longest sequence in a batch to finish, wasting GPU on finished requests. Continuous (iteration-level) batching, pioneered by ORCA and popularized by vLLM, inserts new requests into the batch as soon as any slot frees — at each decode iteration. Combined with chunked prefill, it keeps the GPU saturated under bursty traffic and typically multiplies throughput 5-20x over naive batching.

demo.title: Static vs continuous batching
demo.program:
reqs = [10, 50, 30, 20]  # output lengths
static = max(reqs) * len(reqs)
cont = sum(reqs)
print(f"static token-slots: {static}, continuous: {cont} "
      f"({static/cont:.1f}x waste)")

title: PagedAttention
summary: Manage KV cache in fixed-size blocks like OS virtual memory — kill fragmentation.
details: KV caches for variable-length sequences fragment GPU memory badly. PagedAttention (vLLM) splits the cache into fixed blocks allocated on demand and mapped through a block table, like virtual memory pages. Fragmentation drops to near zero, memory sharing across beam-search candidates becomes trivial, and larger batches fit. It is the memory manager inside vLLM and the reason vLLM serves so many concurrent requests.

demo.title: Fragmentation without paging
demo.program:
import random
random.seed(0)
mem, blocks = 100, []
for _ in range(20):
    need = random.randint(3, 12)
    blocks.append(need)
used = sum(blocks)
print(f"requested {used}/100 but worst-fit leaves gaps; "
      f"paged: waste < 1 block per sequence")

title: Speculative Decoding
summary: Draft tokens with a small model, verify with the big one — same output, much faster.
details: Speculative decoding uses a cheap draft model (or the base model's own heads, as in Medusa/EAGLE) to propose K tokens, then the large model verifies them in one forward pass, accepting the matching prefix. Because verification is parallel, accepted tokens cost a fraction of sequential decoding. Typical speedups are 2-3x with identical outputs (it is lossless — the target model's distribution is preserved). Draft quality determines the win.

demo.title: Expected speedup from acceptance rate
demo.program:
draft_cost, verify_cost = 0.15, 1.0  # relative to one target step
for accept in [0.5, 0.7, 0.85]:
    k = 4
    expected_tokens = sum(accept**i for i in range(k)) + accept**k
    speedup = expected_tokens / (draft_cost * k + verify_cost)
    print(f"accept={accept}: {speedup:.2f}x")

provenance: Leviathan et al.; Chen et al. (2023)

title: Tensor Parallelism
summary: Shard each layer's matrices across GPUs so big models fit and run fast.
details: Tensor (model) parallelism splits individual layers — typically attention heads and MLP shards — across GPUs within a node, with all-reduce/all-gather at layer boundaries over NVLink. It is how 70B+ models fit across multiple GPUs with low latency: each GPU holds 1/N of the weights. Megatron-LM's column/row-parallel linear layers are the canonical implementation; serving engines configure TP degree to match the NVLink domain (usually 8).

demo.title: TP memory per GPU
demo.program:
params_b, tp = 70, 8
print(f"70B fp16 = 140 GB -> {140/tp:.1f} GB/GPU at TP={tp} (+KV cache)")

title: Pipeline Parallelism
summary: Put different layers on different GPUs — simple, but mind the pipeline bubbles.
details: Pipeline parallelism assigns contiguous layer ranges to each GPU; micro-batches flow through the stages. It needs no fast interconnect between stages (activations only cross stage boundaries), so it suits multi-node serving, but pipeline bubbles idle GPUs when micro-batch counts are low. For inference it is usually combined with tensor parallelism: TP within fast nodes, PP across slower links.
benefit: Scale across nodes without fast fabric

demo.title: Pipeline bubble fraction
demo.program:
stages, microbatches = 4, 8
bubble = (stages - 1) / (microbatches + stages - 1)
print(f"bubble idle: {bubble:.1%} (more microbatches -> smaller)")

title: AWQ Quantization
summary: Activation-aware 4-bit weight quantization — near-FP16 quality, ~4x smaller weights.
details: AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) observes that a few salient weight channels matter far more; it scales those channels up before quantizing weights to INT4, protecting them from quantization error. The result: 4-bit weights with minimal perplexity loss, no retraining, and fast INT4 kernels. It is a top choice for serving 70B-class models on limited GPUs.

demo.title: Weight memory: fp16 vs INT4

title: GPTQ Quantization
summary: Layer-wise 4-bit quantization using approximate second-order information.
details: GPTQ quantizes weights layer by layer, using inverse-Hessian information to choose rounding that minimizes layer-output error, processing columns in order with error compensation. One-shot (no retraining), fast to apply, and supported everywhere — GPTQ was the first widely used 4-bit format for LLM serving and remains a baseline every new quant method is compared against.

demo.title: Quantization error sketch
demo.program:
import torch
w = torch.randn(1000)
q = (torch.round(w * 8) / 8)  # fake 4-bit-ish
print("mse:", round(float(((w - q)**2).mean()), 5))

title: GGUF Quantization
summary: llama.cpp's CPU/GPU-friendly quantized format — run big models on consumer hardware.
details: GGUF is llama.cpp's file format bundling quantized weights (Q4_K_M, Q5_K, Q8_0, ...) with metadata. K-quants use super-blocks with per-block scales for better quality than naive 4-bit. GGUF made 70B models runnable on a MacBook or a single 24GB GPU, and the format's ubiquity (Hugging Face hosts thousands of GGUFs) made it the lingua franca of local LLM inference.

demo.title: Quantize a model to Q4_K_M
demo.program:
llama-quantize ./model-f16.gguf ./model-q4k.gguf Q4_K_M
# then: llama-cli -m ./model-q4k.gguf -p "Hello"

title: vLLM
summary: The open serving engine that made PagedAttention and continuous batching standard.
details: vLLM (UC Berkeley) is the most widely deployed open LLM serving engine: PagedAttention memory management, continuous batching, tensor parallelism, quantization (AWQ/GPTQ), LoRA serving, and an OpenAI-compatible API. It routinely delivers 10x+ throughput over Hugging Face pipelines. If you serve open models on GPUs, vLLM is the default answer.

demo.title: Serve a model with vLLM
demo.program:
pip install vllm
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model meta-llama/Llama-3-8B-Instruct --tensor-parallel-size 2

title: Text Generation Inference (TGI)
summary: Hugging Face's production serving toolkit — the engine behind Inference Endpoints.
details: TGI is Hugging Face's Rust+Python serving stack: continuous batching, tensor parallelism, quantization, and streaming via server-sent events, packaged for Inference Endpoints and self-hosting. Its message-API and tooling (benchmark scripts, Docker images) make it the polished, batteries-included alternative to vLLM, especially inside the Hugging Face ecosystem.

demo.title: Run TGI in Docker
demo.program:
docker run --gpus all -p 8080:80 \
  ghcr.io/huggingface/text-generation-inference:latest \
  --model-id bigscience/bloom-560m

title: TensorRT-LLM
summary: NVIDIA's inference compiler: kernel-fused, CUDA-graph-optimized serving for NVIDIA GPUs.
details: TensorRT-LLM compiles models into optimized engines with fused attention kernels, in-flight batching, and CUDA graphs, squeezing maximum throughput from NVIDIA GPUs. It supports the full optimization menu (quantization, speculative decoding, disaggregated serving) and powers NVIDIA NIM microservices. The trade-off is build complexity: engines are compiled per GPU architecture.

demo.title: Engine build sketch (conceptual)
demo.program:
print("trtllm-build --checkpoint_dir ./ckpt "
       "--output_dir ./engine --max_batch_size 32")

title: SGLang
summary: Structured generation language with RadixAttention — fast serving plus constrained decoding.
details: SGLang (UC Berkeley) pairs a high-throughput serving runtime (RadixAttention for prefix-cache reuse across requests, continuous batching) with a frontend language for structured generation (JSON schemas, regex constraints, multi-turn programs). It is the choice when you need both speed and guaranteed output structure — agents and tool-calling pipelines.

demo.title: SGLang structured generation

title: Disaggregated Prefill/Decode
summary: Split prompt processing and token generation onto different GPUs — each phase gets ideal batching.
details: Prefill (processing the prompt) is compute-bound and likes big batches; decode (generating tokens) is memory-bound and likes many sequences. Disaggregated serving (Splitwise, DistServe) puts them on separate GPU pools, transferring KV cache between phases. Each pool can then use its optimal batching, raising overall throughput 1.5-2x on mixed workloads.

demo.title: Phase characteristics
demo.program:
prompt_toks, gen_toks = 2000, 200
print(f"prefill: {prompt_toks} tokens, compute-bound, parallel")
print(f"decode: {gen_toks} steps, memory-bound, sequential")

title: Prefix Caching
summary: Reuse KV cache for shared prompt prefixes — system prompts and few-shot examples computed once.
details: Many requests share prefixes (system prompts, few-shot examples, RAG templates). Prefix caching stores the KV cache for common prefixes and reuses it, skipping redundant prefill compute. With RadixAttention (SGLang) or vLLM's automatic prefix caching, shared-prefix workloads see large TTFT (time-to-first-token) reductions and higher throughput.
benefit: Skip redundant prefill on shared prefixes

demo.title: Prefix hit-rate math
demo.program:
reqs, shared_prefix_toks, total_toks = 1000, 1500, 2000
saved = reqs * shared_prefix_toks
print(f"saved prefill tokens: {saved:,} "
      f"({saved/(reqs*total_toks):.0%} of prefill work)")

title: Chunked Prefill
summary: Split long prompts into chunks interleaved with decode steps — bounded latency for everyone.
details: Long prompts stall decode for all batched requests (prefill is one big matrix multiply). Chunked prefill splits prompts into fixed chunks processed across iterations, interleaved with decode steps, bounding the latency added to any iteration. It is what lets vLLM-class engines mix 32K prompts with interactive chat without latency spikes.
benefit: Long prompts stop stalling interactive requests

demo.title: Chunked vs monolithic prefill
demo.program:
prompt, chunk = 32000, 2048
iters = -(-prompt // chunk)
print(f"{prompt} tokens -> {iters} chunks; "
      f"max added latency per iter ~1 chunk, not {prompt} tokens")

title: FlashAttention
summary: IO-aware exact attention: faster and leaner without changing the math.
details: FlashAttention restructures attention to minimize reads/writes to slow GPU memory (tiling + online softmax), making it 2-4x faster and far more memory-efficient while computing exact attention. FlashAttention-2/3 refine the tiling and add FP8 support. It is not an approximation — outputs are bit-identical to standard attention — which is why it is now default in training and inference alike.

demo.title: Use FlashAttention via PyTorch
demo.program:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
q = k = v = torch.randn(2, 8, 512, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device="cpu")
# on CUDA with backend available:
# out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)  # Flash under the hood
print("SDPA dispatches to FlashAttention/MemEfficient on CUDA")

title: MoE Expert Parallelism
summary: Serve mixture-of-experts models by sharding experts across GPUs.
details: MoE models (Mixtral, DeepSeek) have many experts but activate few per token. Expert parallelism places different experts on different GPUs and routes tokens to them (all-to-all dispatch), so a 100B+ parameter MoE serves with the active cost of a much smaller dense model. Combined with tensor parallelism inside experts, it is the standard MoE serving recipe.
benefit: Serve huge MoEs at small-model active cost

demo.title: MoE active vs total params
demo.program:
total, active = 141e9, 39e9  # Mixtral-8x22B-ish
print(f"total {total/1e9:.0f}B, active {active/1e9:.0f}B "
      f"({active/total:.0%} active per token)")

title: Multi-LoRA Serving
summary: Serve hundreds of LoRA adapters on one base model with punched-in adapter batching.
details: Instead of one GPU per fine-tune, multi-LoRA serving (vLLM, SGLang, LoRAX) keeps one base model in memory and batches requests across many adapters, applying each adapter's low-rank update only to its requests' tokens. Punched kernels make this efficient. It turns 'one model per customer' from a GPU-count problem into a scheduling problem.
benefit: 100s of fine-tunes on one GPU set

demo.title: Adapter memory math
demo.program:
base_gb, per_lora_gb, n = 140, 0.5, 200
print(f"separate: {n} x {base_gb}GB impossible; "
      f"multi-LoRA: {base_gb + n*per_lora_gb:.0f} GB total")

title: Request Prioritization
summary: Schedule interactive requests ahead of batch jobs — SLO-aware serving.
details: Production serving mixes latency-sensitive chat with throughput-oriented batch jobs. Prioritization schedulers (as in Sarathi-Serve) rank requests by deadline/SLO class, preempting or deferring lower-priority work. Combined with chunked prefill, it delivers p99 latency guarantees while keeping batch throughput high.

demo.title: Priority queue order
demo.program:
import heapq
reqs = [("batch", 3), ("chat", 1), ("batch", 3), ("chat", 1)]
hq = [(p, i, r) for i, (r, p) in enumerate(reqs)]
heapq.heapify(hq)
print([heapq.heappop(hq)[2] for _ in range(len(hq))])

title: OpenAI-Compatible Serving API
summary: The de-facto serving protocol: /v1/chat/completions everywhere.
details: OpenAI's chat-completions API shape became the industry standard: vLLM, TGI, SGLang, LM Studio, Ollama, and countless providers expose it, so clients written once work against any backend. The protocol covers chat, completions, embeddings, streaming, tool calls, and structured output — the interoperability layer of the LLM serving world.
benefit: One client works with every backend

demo.title: Call any OpenAI-compatible server
demo.program:
# pip install openai
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="x")
print("POST /v1/chat/completions with model, messages, stream=True")

title: LMDeploy
summary: High-throughput serving with persistent batching and PyTorch-native deployment.
details: LMDeploy (OpenMMLab) offers persistent batching, blocked KV cache, tensor parallelism, and quantization in a PyTorch-friendly package, with a Turbomind C++ backend for maximum speed. Strong in the Chinese open-model ecosystem and competitive with vLLM on throughput, it is a solid alternative engine with good InternLM/Qwen support.

demo.title: Serve with LMDeploy
demo.program:
pip install lmdeploy
lmdeploy serve api_server internlm/internlm2-chat-7b --server-port 23333

title: Medusa Speculative Decoding
summary: Multi-head draft speculation built into the model — no separate draft model needed.
details: Medusa adds extra decoding heads to the target model itself, each predicting tokens 2..K ahead in one forward pass; candidates form a tree verified in parallel by the base model with tree attention. No separate draft model to train or serve, and typical speedups of 2-3x. EAGLE refines the idea with a learned draft head on features. Both ship in major engines.

demo.title: Medusa tree candidates
demo.program:
heads, topk = 3, 2
cands = topk ** heads
print(f"{heads} heads x top-{topk}: {cands} tree candidates verified in parallel")

title: Serverless GPU Inference
summary: GPUs that scale to zero: pay per request, no servers to manage.
details: Serverless GPU platforms (Modal, RunPod Serverless, Baseten, together.ai endpoints) spin GPUs up per request and bill by the second. Cold starts (model load time) are the enemy — mitigated by kept-warm pools and fast loaders. Ideal for bursty workloads where provisioned GPUs would idle; uneconomical for sustained high traffic versus dedicated serving.
benefit: Zero idle cost; infinite burst scaling

demo.title: Serverless cost crossover
demo.program:
reqs_day, sec_per_req, per_sec = 10000, 5, 0.0005
serverless = reqs_day * sec_per_req * per_sec
dedicated = 3.0 * 24  # one H100, $3/hr
print(f"serverless ${serverless:.0f}/day vs dedicated ${dedicated:.0f}/day")

title: KV Cache Quantization
summary: Compress the KV cache to INT8/INT4 — longer contexts and bigger batches in the same VRAM.
details: KV cache often dominates memory at long contexts. Quantizing K and V to INT8 (per-token scales) or INT4 (as in KIVI, Gear) cuts cache size 2-4x with negligible quality loss, directly extending max context or batch size. vLLM and TensorRT-LLM expose FP8/INT8 KV cache options; it composes with PagedAttention and prefix caching.

demo.title: KV cache: fp16 vs int8
demo.program:
layers, hidden, seq, batch = 32, 4096, 32768, 4
for name, b in [("fp16", 2), ("int8", 1)]:
    gb = 2 * layers * hidden * b * seq * batch / 1e9
    print(f"{name}: {gb:.1f} GB")
